sentences.text: Meet Maya.
Maya is a research scientist in the genomics group.
Over the years she has taught her AI agent a few things only she knows: how to read the group's assay results, which cohort definitions to trust, how to summarize a study the way the team expects.
These are skills: small packages of know-how that turn a question into a reliable answer.
The question is how Maya shares them with the whole organization, without becoming a software engineer.
The answer is Skills Hub.
Everything happens through the agent itself.
Installing.
Updating.
Submitting a change.
Sending feedback.
Maya asks in plain language, and the agent runs the tooling.
Google Drive is the hub, and the agent reaches it through the host's Drive connector: in Claude Code, in Cursor, and in Claude Science, on Mac, Windows, or Linux.
Skills travel in packages, arranged in three layers.
Skills Hub itself is the framework: the plumbing for install, sync, publish, and feedback.
The foundation package is the organization's shared ground: skills that know its data sources, its vocabulary, and its internal systems, so every agent starts from the same understanding.
Domain packages extend that foundation for one field, like genomics or clinical research, and they are maintained by the experts in that field.
Each layer has its own version and releases on its own schedule.
Inside a package, a skill is just a folder.
A short instruction file tells the agent when to use it and how.
At least one worked example shows a question, the steps, and the expected answer.
A change log records every submission.
Scripts are optional.
When present, they only read local files or input and print a result.
They never fetch data and they never hold credentials.
Packages live on Google Shared Drives, behind the organization's single sign-on.
Each package has a published drive that everyone can read, and a submissions drive where authors send their changes.
Skills Hub has a published drive of its own, with the START HERE document and an index of every package.
Nothing new to provision, and the agent already knows how to talk to Drive.
Here is the quick start.
One: connect Google Drive in your host.
Two: tell your agent to read the START HERE document on the Skills Hub drive and follow it.
The agent installs Skills Hub, then the foundation package and the domain packages you name, checking each download against its fingerprint.
Three: ask the agent to run doctor.
It reports every installed version and anything that needs attention.
From then on, your agent has the organization's skills.
Staying current works the same way.
Every package has one small pointer file that names the latest version and its fingerprint.
The agent reads the pointer, downloads the release, and verifies the fingerprint byte for byte.
Only a verified release replaces the current one, and the previous version is kept.
If the check fails, nothing changes.
Stale skills stop themselves: a package's scripts refuse to run when it has not been checked for a day, or an update is waiting, and they tell the agent to sync.
In Claude Code, a reminder also appears at the start of each session.
When Maya improves a skill, she tells the agent to publish it.
The agent runs the structure checks, asks why the skill changed, and records the reason in the change log.
It then packages the skill, uploads it to the package's inbox, and downloads it back to confirm that the copy matches.
Maya is also a maintainer of the genomics package, so submissions from colleagues come to her.
For each one, the review tool prints a single report: who submitted it, who owns the skill, the stated reason, the exact difference from the current release, and the results of the checks.
The checks have two levels.
Broken structure blocks a submission: a missing example, no dated change entry, a dependency without an exact version, or anything that looks like a credential.
Everything else is a warning for the reviewer to weigh, such as a script that talks to the network, or a third-party dependency.
The tools do not judge the content.
The maintainer reads the instructions as carefully as the code, because the instructions are what the agent will follow.
Then she accepts or rejects, with a short note that the author's agent can read, and accepted changes go into the next release.
Accepted changes are committed to the package's repo and go out in the next release.
Maya bumps the version; the release tool builds the zip, adds the sync gate to every script, and refuses anything the checks block.
The zip is uploaded, and the pointer file is rewritten last, so a half-uploaded release is never pointed at.
The next sync brings genomics 0.6.0 to everyone who has the package.
Feedback is one sentence.
A colleague tells their agent that a skill gave an odd answer.
The agent asks which skill, asks for consent, and writes a small note to the package's feedback folder.
The maintainers collect those notes into a sheet, and the next release improves.
The design keeps each boundary narrow.
A maintainer can write only to their own package.
Only Skills Hub carries the installer; a content package that tries to include one is refused.
Scripts work on local files and never hold credentials.
And every download is verified against its fingerprint before it is used.
That is Skills Hub.
Three layers.
Shared drives you already have.
Get skills, stay current, and contribute, by asking your agent.
Feedback in one sentence.
One report for every review, and the next sync brings each release to everyone.
Your expertise, available to every agent in the organization.
